newsitem.title: USA: U.S. welcomes results of IMF talks on Thailand aid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. welcomes results of IMF talks on Thailand aid.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Monday the United States was pleased at the outcome of International Monetary Fund talks in Tokyo that agreed on a multi-billion-dollar aid package for economically ailing Thailand.
"We welcome the results of the IMF conference in Tokyo today to discuss multilateral and bilateral financing for Thailand's economic recovery program," Rubin said in a prepared statement.

The international community pledged a total of $16 billion in loans from the IMF and Asian nations, led by Japan, to help Thailand try to achieve financial stability. The money will provide it with the means to plug financial holes created when it floated its baht currency last month after failing to defend it from speculative attacks.
"The United States looks forward to a rapid conclusion of technical discussions between the Thai authorities and the IMF and the presentation of the adjustment program to the IMF Board," Rubin said.
Rubin said previously that the United States did not pledge individual aid, but would support the package to help Thailand through the IMF.
"We also support the expected participation of the Asian development Bank and the World bank, and look forward to learning the details of their proposed financing programs," Rubin said.

The Thai government last week announced an austerity package to meet IMF demands, raising its value-added tax, announcing plans to cut its current account deficit and closing more than half of its financial institutions.
On Monday, Thailand's cabinet approved a broad outline to cut its 1997/98 budget by $1.6 billion to $2.3 billion and will review details on Aug. 19, a government spokesman in Bangkok said.
Thailand's sharp economic slowdown has reduced its tax revenue and is yielding the nation's first budget deficits in a decade this year and in fiscal 1997/98.
